chunks: Driving a motor, isolation and speed control. The question: Draw a circuit to drive a motor from a microcontroller. What if isolation is required?
What if I want to change the speed?
A motor draws far more current than a microcontroller pin can give, especially when starting or stalled.
Its coils of wire also resist any sudden change in current, so when you switch it off it pushes back with a voltage spike.
So the pin only controls a transistor switch, a diode absorbs the spike, and extra parts handle direction, speed and sometimes electrical isolation.
Picture water rushing through a long pipe, with momentum. If you slam the valve shut, the water hammers against it and pressure spikes.
A bypass pipe beside the valve lets the flow keep circulating, and the spike goes away. In the motor, the current is the flow, and the diode is that bypass pipe.
The MOSFET switches the motor's ground return.
The Schottky diode D₁ sits across the motor with its cathode on the supply side: when Q₁ turns off, the motor current continues through D₁ instead of forcing the drain voltage up.
Without D₁ the drain would spike far above 12 volts.
MOSFET: a transistor used as a switch. A small voltage on its gate pin switches a large current.
Flyback diode: a diode across the motor that gives the current a path when the switch opens.
H-bridge: four switches arranged around the motor so you can reverse the voltage across it, and so its direction.
PWM: ("What you can do with timers"): switching on and off quickly, where the on-time fraction (duty cycle) sets the average power.
Stall current: the current when the motor is held still, which is the supply voltage divided by the winding resistance.
Say a 12 volts motor has 2 ohms of winding resistance. Held stalled, it draws 12 / 2 = 6 amps, hundreds of times what a pin can supply.
So the pin drives a MOSFET that switches the motor to ground, with a flyback diode across the motor.
Switching it with PWM at 50% duty gives an average of about 6 volts, so it spins at a little under half its full speed. That is the whole idea.

"For one direction I'd use a logic-level N-MOSFET as a low-side switch, gate through about 100 ohms with a pull-down, and a flyback diode across the motor to catch the inductive kick, plus a bulk capacitor.
For direction, an H-bridge with dead time to avoid shoot-through. For speed, PWM at around 20 kilohertz so the average voltage is duty times supply, ideally with encoder feedback.
If isolation is needed, optocouplers or digital isolators on the control signals, with an isolated gate driver and isolated supply on the power side."
